title: Acute asthma in children
subject: paediatrics
setting: Primary care, emergency department, ward, PICU
summary: Assess severity, give salbutamol by pMDI and spacer repeated every 20 to 30 minutes in the first hour, and oral prednisolone 1 to 2 mg/kg (max 20 mg under 2 years, 30 mg at 2 to 5 years, 40 mg at 6 to 11 years). Add ipratropium for moderate to severe attacks and IV magnesium 40 to 50 mg/kg (max 2 g) if not responding (GINA 2026, BTS/SIGN).

sections.title: Assess severity (BTS/SIGN)
items: Moderate: talks in sentences, SpO2 92% or more, heart rate 140/min or less (1 to 5 years) or 125/min or less (over 5 years), respiratory rate 40/min or less (1 to 5 years) or 30/min or less (over 5 years).

Severe: cannot complete sentences or too breathless to talk or feed, SpO2 below 92%, PEF 33 to 50% of best or predicted, heart rate above 140 (1 to 5 years) or 125 (over 5 years), respiratory rate above 40 (1 to 5 years) or 30 (over 5 years).
Life-threatening: SpO2 below 92% plus any of exhaustion, hypotension, cyanosis, silent chest, poor respiratory effort, confusion, or PEF below 33%.

If there are features of anaphylaxis (sudden onset after food, sting or drug, urticaria, hypotension), give IM adrenaline first. Under 12 months, wheeze is usually bronchiolitis and responds poorly to bronchodilators.

sections.title: First hour
items: Oxygen only if SpO2 is below 92%. GINA 2026 target on oxygen: 92 to 95% (6 to 11 years) and 92% or more (5 years and under). BTS/SIGN uses 94 to 98% in severe attacks; this protocol follows GINA.

Salbutamol 100 mcg per puff by pMDI and spacer (with face mask under 3 years), one puff at a time with 5 to 6 breaths each: 4 puffs for mild attacks; 4 to 6 puffs (up to 10 in severe attacks per BTS/SIGN) every 20 to 30 minutes, up to 3 times in the first hour.
If a spacer cannot be used or the attack is severe or life-threatening: nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg (2.5 to 5 mg in older children, BTS/SIGN), oxygen-driven if hypoxic, every 20 to 30 minutes.

Moderate to severe attacks or poor response: add ipratropium 4 puffs of 20 mcg by spacer or 250 mcg nebulised with each salbutamol dose, every 20 to 30 minutes for up to 3 doses in the first hour or two. There is no benefit after the first 1 to 2 hours.

Give systemic steroids early for moderate to severe attacks: oral prednisolone 1 to 2 mg/kg once daily (max 20 mg under 2 years, 30 mg at 2 to 5 years, 40 mg at 6 to 11 years) for 3 to 5 days, or dexamethasone 0.3 to 0.6 mg/kg (max 12 mg) for 1 to 2 days.
If oral steroids cannot be taken or kept down: IV hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg (max 100 mg) every 4 to 6 hours (BTS/SIGN) or IV methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg every 6 hours on day 1 (GINA).

sections.title: Severe or not responding after the first hour
items: IV magnesium sulphate 40 to 50 mg/kg (max 2 g) as a single infusion over 20 minutes for children aged 2 years or more with severe asthma or SpO2 below 92% after first-line treatment (GINA 2026; BTS/SIGN 40 mg/kg). 50% solution is 500 mg/mL; dilute before use.

IV salbutamol: single bolus 15 mcg/kg over 10 minutes in a severe attack not responding to inhaled therapy; continuous infusion 1 to 2 mcg/kg/min in HDU with ECG and electrolyte monitoring, up to 5 mcg/kg/min only in PICU (BTS/SIGN).

IV aminophylline only for severe or life-threatening asthma unresponsive to maximal bronchodilators and steroids, after senior review: 5 mg/kg over 20 minutes (omit if on oral theophylline), then 1 mg/kg/h with ECG monitoring.

Keep giving frequent inhaled bronchodilators during IV therapy. Check potassium and consider lactate: salbutamol toxicity causes tachycardia, tremor, hypokalaemia and lactic acidosis with fast breathing that can be mistaken for worsening asthma.
Do not routinely give antibiotics, sedatives or chest physiotherapy. Nebulised magnesium is not recommended for mild to moderate attacks.

sections.title: Monitoring and admission
items: Reassess work of breathing, SpO2, heart rate and respiratory rate after each treatment and at 1 hour; measure PEF or FEV1 in children over 5 years who can perform it.

Observe children with a severe attack for at least 1 hour after starting treatment. Admit if there is no response at 1 hour, SpO2 below 92%, salbutamol needed more often than every 1 to 2 hours, or distress persisting 4 to 6 hours after steroids (GINA).
Blood gases are rarely needed; a normal or rising PaCO2 in a distressed child signals respiratory failure.

sections.title: PICU and escalation
items: Life-threatening features, poor response to first-line and IV therapy, rising oxygen need, exhaustion, drowsiness or a silent chest: call senior and PICU teams early and arrange retrieval.
Ventilatory support (non-invasive or intubation) only by experienced staff; ketamine and other rescue therapies belong in critical care.
While awaiting transfer, continue oxygen, frequent or continuous nebulised salbutamol and IV therapy with ECG, potassium and glucose monitoring.

sections.title: Discharge
items: Discharge when signs of severity have resolved, activity and oral intake are normal, and the child has managed at least 3 hours without salbutamol (some can go home at 1 hour after senior review).

Complete the steroid course; start or step up inhaled corticosteroid-containing controller therapy; check inhaler and spacer technique; give a written asthma action plan; review within 2 to 5 days (GINA).
Before discharge, identify triggers (viral infection, smoke exposure, poor adherence) and check that preventer and reliever supplies are affordable and available.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Giving steroids late or in low doses; they take about 4 hours to work.
Using nebulisers when a pMDI with spacer would work as well with fewer side effects.
Escalating salbutamol for fast breathing caused by salbutamol toxicity and lactic acidosis.
Missing a foreign body, pneumothorax, anaphylaxis or heart failure in atypical or non-responding wheeze.

drugs.name: Salbutamol pMDI 100 mcg/puff with spacer
drugs.dose: 4 to 6 puffs (up to 10 in severe attacks) every 20 to 30 minutes, up to 3 times in the first hour, then as needed
drugs.notes: One puff at a time with 5 to 6 tidal breaths each.

drugs.name: Salbutamol nebulised
drugs.dose: 2.5 mg (2.5 to 5 mg in older children) every 20 to 30 minutes
drugs.notes: Oxygen-driven if hypoxic; severe or life-threatening attacks.

drugs.name: Ipratropium bromide
drugs.dose: 4 puffs of 20 mcg by spacer or 250 mcg nebulised with salbutamol, every 20 to 30 minutes for up to 3 doses
drugs.notes: Moderate to severe attacks, first 1 to 2 hours only.

drugs.name: Prednisolone
drugs.dose: 1 to 2 mg/kg orally once daily for 3 to 5 days (max 20 mg under 2 years, 30 mg at 2 to 5 years, 40 mg at 6 to 11 years)

drugs.name: Dexamethasone
drugs.dose: 0.3 to 0.6 mg/kg orally once daily (max 12 mg) for 1 to 2 days
drugs.notes: Alternative to prednisolone; switch to prednisolone if relapse.

drugs.name: Hydrocortisone
drugs.dose: 4 mg/kg IV (max 100 mg) every 4 to 6 hours
drugs.notes: Only if unable to take or retain oral steroids.

drugs.name: Magnesium sulphate
drugs.dose: 40 to 50 mg/kg IV (max 2 g) over 20 minutes, single dose
drugs.notes: Age 2 years or more with severe asthma not responding to first-line treatment.

drugs.name: Salbutamol IV
drugs.dose: 15 mcg/kg over 10 minutes as a single bolus; infusion 1 to 2 mcg/kg/min (up to 5 mcg/kg/min in PICU)

drugs.name: Aminophylline
drugs.dose: 5 mg/kg IV over 20 minutes, then 1 mg/kg/h
drugs.notes: Omit loading dose if on oral theophylline; senior decision, ECG monitoring.

sources.title: Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention, 2026 update (chapters on exacerbations and children 5 years and younger)
SIGN 158: British guideline on the management of asthma (acute asthma in children)
